lessons.title: Your first symbolic expression
lessons.short: Construct an expression and recognise its mathematical meaning.
lessons.goal: Construct an expression and recognise its mathematical meaning.
explain: A symbolic expression represents a calculation without requiring a numerical value for every quantity. SymPy keeps the symbol $x$ inside the result, so you can transform the expression before choosing a value for $x$.

The mathematics $(x+1)^2$ squares the entire sum. In Python, write `(x+1)**2`: parentheses group the sum and `**` means a power. Multiplication needs an explicit `*`. Importing `sympy as sp` gives a short, consistent prefix for SymPy’s functions.

Run the example and compare the original expression with its expanded form. Both describe the same polynomial. The `results` dictionary labels the expressions displayed by this lab; the final loop also prints them when you download and run the file locally.

refresher.title: Squares and brackets
refresher.body: Squaring a sum multiplies the whole sum by itself. The middle terms do not disappear.
refresher.example: At $x=2$, both forms give 9. Squaring each term separately would give 5 and changes the expression.

lessons.predict: Will $(x+1)^2$ and $x^2+1$ expand to the same polynomial?
lessons.look: The result keeps a symbol rather than guessing a number. Both forms include the cross term $2x$: the two rectangles in the area model explain where it comes from.
lessons.change: Change 1 to 2 inside the brackets. Predict the middle and constant terms before running.
lessons.question: Which Python expression means the square of the sum of x and 3?
lessons.feedback: Parentheses group the sum and `**` raises it to a power. Python `^` is a bitwise operator, not the power operator.
hints: Decide what the exponent applies to.
Use `**` after the complete bracketed sum.
lessons.limit: Expansion changes form. It does not assign a value to x or solve an equation.

lessons.title: Keep numbers exact
lessons.short: Choose exact rational inputs before Python rounds a calculation.
lessons.goal: Choose exact rational inputs before Python rounds a calculation.
explain: A rational number is an exact ratio of integers. In ordinary Python, dividing two integers with / produces a floating-point approximation. If that division happens before SymPy receives the value, the exact fraction has already been replaced.

Use `Rational(1,3)` or `S(1)/3` to construct an exact third. SymPy then carries the fraction through algebra without rounding. A `Float` can be useful for approximate measurements, but it represents a different kind of input from an exact rational.

Compare the two sums below. An approximate result may look convincingly like one on screen while retaining a small numerical difference internally. Choose exactness from the provenance of the input: a mathematical third can be exact; a measured decimal normally has its own uncertainty.

refresher.title: Fractions as numbers
refresher.body: A fraction $\frac ab$ means a divided by a nonzero b. Equivalent fractions represent the same number.
refresher.example: Three exact thirds make one. Writing 0.333 three times instead gives 0.999; extra printed digits do not restore the discarded information.

lessons.predict: Does passing the already calculated Python value 1/3 to SymPy recover an exact third?
lessons.look: The stored float corresponds to a nearby binary fraction. Converting that stored value back to an exact fraction exposes the difference; it does not recover the intended third.
lessons.change: Compare `sp.Rational("0.1")` with `sp.Float(0.1,30)`. Explain why the longer `Float` cannot improve the original Python float.
lessons.question: Which input best represents an exact mathematical two sevenths?
options: `sp.Rational(2,7)`
lessons.feedback: `Rational` receives the exact integers before division. Increasing precision after Python division cannot recover lost input information.
hints: Look for the point where division is first evaluated.
Pass the numerator and denominator separately.
lessons.limit: Exact rational arithmetic does not make uncertain real-world observations exact.

lessons.title: A symbol is an object
lessons.short: Distinguish a symbol from a Python name and from its printed label.
lessons.goal: Distinguish a symbol from a Python name and from its printed label.
explain: A Python variable is a name referring to an object. A SymPy `Symbol` is an object representing an unspecified quantity. Reassigning the Python name later does not rewrite expressions already built from that symbol.

Symbols also carry assumptions. Two symbols can print with the same label but differ because one is positive and another has no such assumption. Mixing them accidentally can leave expressions that look simpler than their internal structure really is.

Construct symbols once and reuse those objects consistently. The example retains the original symbol in `saved_x`, then reassigns the Python name x. Inspect the expression’s `free_symbols` to identify the mathematical quantities that remain inside it.

refresher.title: Variables and values
refresher.body: A mathematical variable can stand for many permitted values. A Python assignment binds a name now; it is not an equation to solve.
refresher.example: If f is built using a symbol x, later assigning the Python name `x=10` does not replace x inside that already-built symbolic object.

lessons.predict: After `x=10`, will an earlier expression built from the symbol x automatically become a number?
lessons.look: The printed symbol inside expression remains. Explicit substitution uses the saved symbol object.
lessons.change: Use a different printed label for `positive_x`, then compare `free_symbols` and equality again.
lessons.question: An expression unexpectedly contains two symbols printed as t. What should you inspect?
options: Only the font used to print t.
Their assumptions and whether the same symbol objects were reused.
Whether Python assignment used spaces.
lessons.feedback: Names on screen do not expose all symbol metadata. Consistent construction and `free_symbols` help diagnose mismatches.
hints: A printed label is only part of a `Symbol`.
Compare assumptions and object equality.
lessons.limit: This lesson addresses ordinary symbolic objects, not every advanced binding or scoping construct in SymPy.

lessons.title: Tell SymPy what a symbol means
lessons.short: Use domain assumptions to justify a square-root simplification.
lessons.goal: Use domain assumptions to justify a square-root simplification.
explain: An identity must hold for all values permitted by its assumptions. SymPy therefore cannot generally replace the square root of x squared by x. Negative real values already provide a counterexample.

With `real=True`, the expression becomes `Abs(x)`, the nonnegative distance of x from zero. With `positive=True`, the symbol is strictly positive, so that absolute value reduces to the symbol itself. An unconstrained symbol can represent complex values and needs additional care.

Assumptions belong in the model before simplification. Do not add positivity merely to obtain a shorter answer. Compare the three outputs and substitute a negative real value into the real-symbol expression to see why the distinction matters.

refresher.title: Square roots and absolute value
refresher.body: The principal square root of a nonnegative real number is nonnegative. Absolute value is a number’s distance from zero.
refresher.example: For $x=-3$, $\sqrt{x^2}=\sqrt9=3$, while $x$ itself is $-3$. For a positive $x$, $|x|=x$.

lessons.predict: Should `sqrt(x**2)` simplify the same way for unrestricted, real and positive symbols?
lessons.look: The different outputs preserve different sets of permitted inputs.
lessons.change: Replace `positive=True` with `nonnegative=True`. Then try `negative=True` using a new symbol.
lessons.question: A formula must work for any real displacement, including negative values. Which reduction is justified?
options: `sqrt(x**2)` becomes `x`.
`sqrt(x**2)` becomes `-x`.
`sqrt(x**2)` becomes `Abs(x)`.
lessons.feedback: `Abs(x)` covers both signs. A displacement’s sign cannot be discarded by assuming it is positive.
hints: Test $x=-1$ and $x=1$.
Choose a form that is nonnegative in both cases.
lessons.limit: Assumptions are mathematical restrictions supplied by you; SymPy does not establish their real-world truth.

lessons.title: Substitute deliberately
lessons.short: Replace symbols explicitly and distinguish simultaneous substitution from sequential updates.
lessons.goal: Replace symbols explicitly and distinguish simultaneous substitution from sequential updates.
explain: Substitution replaces an expression or symbol inside another expression. It creates a new object; the original expression is unchanged. Use the symbol objects you actually used when constructing the expression.

Order matters when replacements depend on one another. Sequentially changing x to y and then y to x is not a reliable way to swap their original roles. `simultaneous=True` applies replacements `together` without using one replacement as input to another.

Inspect the original, ordinary sequential replacement and simultaneous swap below. This matters when renaming variables, changing coordinates or substituting several model inputs. Retain a copy of the symbolic formula before inserting particular numbers.

refresher.title: Functions with several inputs
refresher.body: A formula can depend on more than one independent quantity. Replacing an input means evaluating or rewriting that particular role.
refresher.example: At $x=1$ and $y=3$, $f(x,y)=7$, whereas swapping the input roles gives $f(y,x)=5$.

lessons.predict: Will sequential replacements x→y and y→x necessarily swap the two original symbols?
lessons.look: The original remains $x+2y$. A simultaneous swap preserves the two distinct roles.
lessons.change: Swap symbols in $\frac xy$. Compare sequential and simultaneous replacement without assuming the denominator is always nonzero.
lessons.question: Which operation safely swaps the original roles of a and b?
options: `expr.subs(a,b).subs(b,a)`
Assigning the Python name `a=b`.
`expr.subs({a:b,b:a}, simultaneous=True)`
lessons.feedback: Simultaneous replacement avoids cascading the first replacement into the second. Keep the expression’s domain restrictions too.
hints: A swap must retain both original roles.
Use the simultaneous option.
lessons.limit: Substitution does not automatically preserve or document every domain restriction of a transformed formula.

lessons.title: Choose when to approximate
lessons.short: Evaluate an exact expression numerically at a chosen precision.
lessons.goal: Evaluate an exact expression numerically at a chosen precision.
explain: Exact forms such as $\sqrt2$ and pi preserve a mathematical definition. Numerical evaluation turns them into approximations with a requested number of significant digits. Use `evalf` or N when a decimal answer serves the question.

Precision means how many digits the arithmetic carries, not how much real-world evidence supports an input. A high-precision result from a low-precision measurement is still limited by that measurement. Avoid confusing the number of printed decimal places with significant digits.

The example retains an exact expression and evaluates it twice. Direct `evalf` with `subs` can also evaluate a formula using high-precision substitution more reliably than doing an early low-precision calculation. Later numerical lessons examine cancellation and input precision in more detail.

refresher.title: Exact values and decimal approximations
refresher.body: Some numbers have no finite decimal representation. A symbolic definition can remain exact while any finite decimal is an approximation.
refresher.example: Rounding $\sqrt2$ to three significant digits gives 1.41. Squaring that rounded value does not give exactly 2.

lessons.predict: Does requesting 40 digits of an exact $\sqrt2$ require replacing it with a Python float first?
lessons.look: The exact check is zero before numerical rounding. The two decimal displays approximate the same exact quantity.
lessons.change: Compare `sp.N(sp.pi,50)` with `sp.N(3.141592653589793,50)`. Explain the input information available in each.
lessons.question: A sensor supplies about four reliable digits. What does printing 50 digits establish?
options: Fifty reliable digits about the physical quantity.
Only a longer numerical representation; it adds no measurement information.
That the model assumptions are correct.
lessons.feedback: Arithmetic precision and evidence precision are different. Preserve both in a report.
hints: Ask where the input came from.
Printing cannot create new observations.
lessons.limit: Numerical precision controls arithmetic representation, not measurement error or model validity.

lessons.title: Expand or factor?
lessons.short: Choose between a sum of terms and a product of factors.
lessons.goal: Choose between a sum of terms and a product of factors.
explain: Expanding distributes products and powers into a sum. Factoring seeks a product representation. Both can represent the same polynomial, but each makes different structure visible.

A product can reveal zeros: if a product of real or complex numbers is zero, at least one factor is zero. A sum of powers is often convenient for reading coefficients or differentiating term by term. Choose the form from the task.

The example starts with a quadratic whose factors are small integers. Verify that expanding the factored result recovers the polynomial. Successful factorisation here is over rational coefficients; other domains or extensions can produce different factorizations.

refresher.title: The distributive law
refresher.body: Multiplication distributes over addition. Factoring applies that relationship in reverse.
refresher.example: The two cross terms are $3x$ and $-2x$, so the coefficient of x is 1. The constant term is -6.

lessons.predict: Which form will make the zeros $x=2$ and $x=-3$ easiest to see?
lessons.look: The zero identity check verifies the algebraic transformation for this polynomial.
lessons.change: Replace the polynomial by `x**2+1`. Compare factor with `factor(..., extension=sp.I)`.
lessons.question: You want to read the coefficient of x cubed. Which representation is usually useful?
options: A fully expanded polynomial in x.
Only a decimal approximation at $x=1$.
Only a plot near zero.
lessons.feedback: Expanded powers expose coefficients. Evaluation at one point cannot recover the whole polynomial structure.
hints: A coefficient multiplies a power of the variable.
Write the expression as a sum of powers.
lessons.limit: A factorisation depends on the coefficient domain. A polynomial irreducible over rationals may factor over complex numbers.

lessons.title: Collect the terms you need
lessons.short: Group an expression by powers of a chosen symbol.
lessons.goal: Group an expression by powers of a chosen symbol.
explain: An expression can contain several symbols. Collecting with respect to one of them groups its powers while treating the others as coefficients. This is useful when a model depends on both an independent variable and adjustable parameters.

Use `collect` after expansion when necessary. The result can expose how strongly each parameter or power contributes without substituting particular values. The `coeff` method extracts the coefficient of a specified power from an appropriate expanded expression.

Below, x is the grouping variable while a and b remain symbolic coefficients. Compare the full expression with the collected form and the coefficient of x. Grouping is a representation choice; it does not change the mathematical value.

refresher.title: Like terms
refresher.body: Terms with the same power of a variable can be combined by adding their coefficients.
refresher.example: For $a=2$ and $b=5$, the two $x$ terms become $7x$. The parameters can remain symbolic while you perform the same grouping.

lessons.predict: When collecting in x, must a and b first be assigned numerical values?
lessons.look: Changing the collection variable changes the visible grouping, not the expression’s value.
lessons.change: Add `b*x**2` and inspect the coefficient of x squared.
lessons.question: In $(a+b)x+3$, what is the coefficient of x?
options: x
$a+b$
lessons.feedback: The whole expression $a+b$ multiplies x. Coefficients can themselves depend on other symbols.
hints: Treat a and b as fixed while grouping by x.
Identify the factor multiplying the first power of x.
lessons.limit: `coeff` is a structural extraction tool; expansion or collection may be needed before asking for a particular coefficient.

lessons.title: Cancel with the domain in view
lessons.short: Simplify a rational expression while retaining its original excluded inputs.
lessons.goal: Simplify a rational expression while retaining its original excluded inputs.
explain: Cancelling common factors can turn a complicated rational expression into a simpler formula. However, a factor that appears in the denominator excludes values where that denominator is zero. Removing its visible occurrence does not restore those inputs to the original problem.

For (x squared minus one) divided by (x minus one), cancellation produces $x+1$. The original expression is undefined at $x=1$; the simplified polynomial is defined there. The formulas agree wherever the original is defined.

Keep the original denominator or a separate domain note when transforming a model. Later, a limit can describe the value approached near an excluded point, but a limit is not the original expression’s value at that point. Domain bookkeeping is part of the answer.

refresher.title: Division by zero and removable holes
refresher.body: A fraction requires a nonzero denominator. Cancelling a common factor preserves equality only where that factor was nonzero.
refresher.example: At $x=2$ both expressions equal 3. At $x=1$ the original becomes 0/0, while the polynomial equals 2.

lessons.predict: Does cancellation prove that the original fraction is defined at $x=1$?
lessons.look: nan marks the indeterminate direct substitution here. The reduced expression supplies a continuation, not a repair of the original domain.
lessons.change: Try `(x**2-4)/(x-2)`, and record the excluded value before cancelling.
lessons.question: A transformed expression agrees with the original except at a cancelled denominator zero. What should a report include?
options: The simpler formula and the original exclusion.
Only the simpler formula, with every real input allowed.
A claim that division by zero is now valid.
lessons.feedback: Algebraic convenience does not erase an original restriction. State the domain beside the transformed formula.
hints: Inspect the denominator before cancellation.
Keep its zeros as exclusions.
lessons.limit: SymPy expressions do not automatically retain a full history of removed domain restrictions.

lessons.title: Separate partial fractions
lessons.short: Rewrite a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions.
lessons.goal: Rewrite a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions.
explain: Partial fractions decompose a rational function into simpler denominator pieces. This can expose contributions, poles or terms that are easier to integrate. The decomposition is an identity on the original domain.

Use `apart` with the intended variable. Treat other symbols as parameters only when the relevant coefficient assumptions support that interpretation. Repeated or irreducible factors can produce different kinds of terms from this first example.

Below, the denominator has factors x and $x+1$. Compare the decomposition with the original by bringing their difference to a common denominator. A zero result verifies the identity away from the poles; it does not make either expression defined at them.

refresher.title: Adding fractions in reverse
refresher.body: Partial fractions reverse common-denominator addition. A rational function is a ratio of polynomials.
refresher.example: Combining the right side gives $\frac{(x+1)-x}{x(x+1)}=\frac1{x(x+1)}$, for $x\ne0,-1$.

lessons.predict: Will the decomposition preserve the excluded values $x=0$ and $x=-1$?
lessons.look: The minus sign on the second term is essential. Inspect it before trusting a remembered pattern.
lessons.change: Use `1/(x*(x+2))` and predict the coefficient of each simple fraction.
lessons.question: Why might partial fractions be useful before integration?
options: They always remove every singularity.
They can expose simpler terms with known antiderivatives.
They turn every rational function into a constant.
lessons.feedback: The representation can make an operation easier while preserving the original domain restrictions.
hints: Think about integrating a sum term by term.
A simple denominator may have a familiar antiderivative.
lessons.limit: This example has distinct linear factors. Higher-degree and repeated factors need a more general decomposition.

lessons.title: Build a common denominator
lessons.short: Combine rational terms into one inspectable fraction.
lessons.goal: Combine rational terms into one inspectable fraction.
explain: Combining fractions is useful when you want a single numerator, denominator or residual. `together` constructs a common-denominator representation. It serves a different representation goal from partial-fraction decomposition.

Use fraction to inspect the resulting numerator and denominator. This makes it easier to analyse zeros and excluded inputs separately. A numerator zero is only a valid zero of the rational function where the denominator remains nonzero.

The example combines two terms that do not share a denominator. Verify the result algebraically and inspect the denominator before interpreting any subsequent solver output. Automated simplification can change visible form, so keep the original problem and its domain nearby.

refresher.title: Common denominators
refresher.body: To add fractions, express them using the same denominator and add their numerators.
refresher.example: The new numerator is $(x+1)+x$. Values $0$ and $-1$ remain excluded because the original terms are undefined there.

lessons.predict: Does the zero of the combined numerator automatically make every denominator input valid?
lessons.look: fraction separates the representation you supplied. It is not a substitute for tracking the original domain.
lessons.change: Combine `1/(x-1)+2/(x+1)` and identify both excluded values.
lessons.question: After combining fractions, what should you check before interpreting a numerator root?
options: Whether the denominator is nonzero there and the original expression is defined.
Only the number of printed terms.
Whether the root is positive.
lessons.feedback: A numerator equal to zero describes a rational zero only where division is allowed. Check that the original expression is defined there.
hints: A fraction has both a numerator and a denominator.
Substitute the candidate into the original problem.
lessons.limit: A convenient combined denominator can conceal removable factors if further cancellation is performed.

lessons.title: Simplify towards a goal
lessons.short: Select a targeted transformation and verify the relationship between forms.
lessons.goal: Select a targeted transformation and verify the relationship between forms.
explain: There is no single best-looking form of every expression. A factored polynomial, expanded sum and trigonometric identity may each suit a different task. simplify applies broad heuristics; targeted functions express a clearer intention.

Use `trigsimp` for trigonometric identities, factor for polynomial products and cancel for rational factors. Comparing structure with `==` asks whether objects have the same representation, not whether every algebraically equivalent pair is written identically.

For suitable expressions, simplifying their difference to zero is a useful identity check. Failure to reach zero is not a proof of inequality: symbolic equivalence is difficult in general. Combine the check with assumptions and domain reasoning, and distinguish identity from agreement at a few numerical points.

refresher.title: Identity versus one example
refresher.body: An identity holds throughout a stated domain. Agreement at one input is weaker evidence.
refresher.example: The difference expands to zero for every x. In contrast, $x^2=x$ happens at $x=0$ and $x=1$ but is not an identity.

lessons.predict: Can two equivalent polynomial expressions compare unequal with structural `==`?
lessons.look: Structural comparison and mathematical equivalence answer different questions.
lessons.change: Compare `x**2` and x at several points, then examine `sp.factor(x**2-x)`.
lessons.question: Two formulas match at $x=0$ and $x=1$. What does that establish?
options: An identity for all complex x.
Agreement at those tested points, requiring more work to establish an identity.
That their Python expression trees are identical.
lessons.feedback: Finite examples can reveal a counterexample but do not generally establish a symbolic identity.
hints: Consider x² and x.
A claim about all inputs needs a reason covering the domain.
lessons.limit: No single simplification or numerical sampling strategy decides equivalence for all possible symbolic expressions.

lessons.title: Write an equation, then solve it
lessons.short: Represent an equality with Eq and verify a computed solution.
lessons.goal: Represent an equality with Eq and verify a computed solution.
explain: An expression is a mathematical object; an equation states that two expressions are equal. Python assignment binds a name, while `Eq` constructs a symbolic equation. Keep those roles separate when translating a word problem.

For a first algebraic equation, solve can return a list of candidate values for the specified symbol. Supply that symbol explicitly. The equation below is linear, so rearranging it by hand provides an independent check of the result.

Substitute each candidate into the original left and right sides, then simplify their difference. This makes verification visible rather than assuming that a printed answer meets every condition. Later lessons use solution sets to express domains and families more explicitly.

refresher.title: Keeping an equality balanced
refresher.body: Applying the same reversible operation to both sides preserves the solutions of an equation.
refresher.example: Subtract 2 from both sides, then divide both sides by the nonzero number 3. Substitution gives $3\cdot3+2=11$.

lessons.predict: Does assigning `equation = ...` itself ask Python to solve the equation?
lessons.look: `Eq` records a relationship; solve performs the solving operation. The residuals check the original relationship.
lessons.change: Change the coefficient 3 to 5 and the right side to 12. Predict the exact rational answer.
lessons.question: Which object represents an equation without assigning a value to the symbol x?
lessons.feedback: `Eq` creates symbolic equality. Assignment rebinds a Python name; `==` tests structural equality.
hints: Distinguish a relationship from a Python operation.
Use the symbolic equality constructor.
lessons.limit: Checking an equation is necessary, but additional domain, sign or physical constraints may still exclude a candidate.

lessons.title: State the solution domain
lessons.short: Use solveset to distinguish real and complex solution sets.
lessons.goal: Use solveset to distinguish real and complex solution sets.
explain: A solving question includes its domain: the set of permitted values. A polynomial can have no real solutions but still have complex ones. State the domain explicitly instead of inferring it from how a symbol is printed.

`solveset` returns a mathematical set, such as `FiniteSet`, `EmptySet` or a more general set description. An empty real solution set means no real value satisfies the equation; it does not mean that the equation is meaningless or that no other domain has solutions.

Solve x squared plus one equal to zero over both reals and complexes. The imaginary unit I satisfies I squared equal to minus one. Future solvers can return `ConditionSet` when a general symbolic answer is unresolved; that is not the same as `EmptySet`.

refresher.title: Real and complex numbers
refresher.body: Real numbers lie on a number line. Complex numbers include the imaginary unit i with $i^2=-1$.
refresher.example: Every real square is nonnegative, so $x^2=-1$ has no real solution. The values i and -i both square to -1.

lessons.predict: Will $x^2+1=0$ have the same solution set over reals and complexes?
lessons.look: Passing an expression to `solveset` means solving that expression equal to zero.
lessons.change: Replace +1 with -1, then compare the two domains again.
lessons.question: What does `EmptySet` from a real-domain solve establish?
options: No solution in the requested real domain.
No complex solution to any related equation.
That the solver failed to run.
lessons.feedback: The domain is part of the claim. `EmptySet` and an unresolved `ConditionSet` carry different meanings.
hints: Read the domain argument alongside the answer.
Restrict the conclusion to the set you asked about.
lessons.limit: Symbolic solvers do not have closed-form answers for every equation; inspect the returned set and verify its interpretation.

lessons.title: Solve a linear system
lessons.short: Interpret linsolve output as a jointly constrained tuple.
lessons.goal: Interpret linsolve output as a jointly constrained tuple.
explain: A system requires all its equations to hold at the same time. Solving each equation separately without connecting shared variables can produce incompatible values. `linsolve` handles linear systems and returns a set of ordered solution tuples.

State the variable order explicitly. A tuple for (x,y) gives the x value first and the y value second, regardless of a story’s naming conventions. Substitute the whole tuple into every original residual to check the system.

The invented ticket problem below has a total count and a total revenue constraint. Its unique solution is exact. Other systems can have no solutions or a family with free parameters; the output set communicates that structure rather than always yielding one pair.

refresher.title: Two equations together
refresher.body: A solution of a system is an input combination satisfying every equation, not one equation at a time.
refresher.example: From the first equation $x=10-y$. Substitution gives $20+y=24$, so $y=4$ and $x=6$.

lessons.predict: Does a pair satisfying only the total-count equation solve the full system?
lessons.look: Each zero residual checks one original equation using the same pair.
lessons.change: Change the revenue 24 to 25, then consider whether the result meets an additional integer ticket-count requirement.
lessons.question: For `linsolve(equations,(u,v))`, how should a result tuple (2,5) be read?
options: One answer for either variable, chosen later.
$u=2$ and $v=5$, jointly.
lessons.feedback: The variable order defines the tuple positions. Both values belong to one joint solution.
hints: Read the ordered symbol tuple in the call.
Keep the values paired during verification.
lessons.limit: Linear algebra solves the mathematical system; integer counts and nonnegativity may impose additional modelling constraints.

lessons.title: Solve a nonlinear system
lessons.short: Keep all branches of a nonlinear system and verify complete candidate pairs.
lessons.goal: Keep all branches of a nonlinear system and verify complete candidate pairs.
explain: Nonlinear equations can have several isolated solutions or larger families. `nonlinsolve` returns sets of tuples so those joint branches remain visible. Do not select a convenient branch before stating which extra conditions justify the selection.

Intersect a circle with a line. Substituting the line relationship into the circle creates a quadratic, so two intersection points are plausible. The example checks both returned pairs against both original residuals.

A physical interpretation may require positive coordinates or a bounded region, but those are extra constraints. Include them explicitly and explain any excluded branch. General nonlinear systems can be much harder, and solver output may contain parameters or unresolved conditions.

refresher.title: Intersections of curves
refresher.body: A common solution of two curve equations is a point lying on both curves.
refresher.example: Substituting $y=x-1$ gives $2x^2-2x-4=0$. The points are $(-1,-2)$ and $(2,1)$.

lessons.predict: Should a solver return only the intersection with positive coordinates when no sign constraint was supplied?
lessons.look: Every candidate is a full coordinate pair. Both pairs satisfy the equations, even if a later application selects one.
lessons.change: Replace the radius-squared value 5 with 1 and examine the changed intersections.
lessons.question: A nonlinear solver finds two valid branches. A model permits only positive x. What next?
options: Apply and document that additional constraint, then verify the retained branch.
Silently discard whichever answer prints second.
Average the two branches into a new solution.
lessons.feedback: A stated model restriction can select a branch. Ordering or averaging is not a mathematical justification.
hints: Separate the equations from extra admissibility conditions.
Check each candidate against the explicit condition.
lessons.limit: This system has finite elementary solutions. General nonlinear solving can return parametric or incomplete symbolic descriptions.

lessons.title: Solve an inequality as a region
lessons.short: Read an inequality solution as intervals with explicit endpoints.
lessons.goal: Read an inequality solution as intervals with explicit endpoints.
explain: An inequality describes a region, not usually a list of isolated roots. Its boundary depends on whether equality is included. Multiplying an inequality by an expression of unknown sign can reverse or invalidate a hand calculation.

`reduce_inequalities` can reduce suitable one-variable inequalities to logical conditions. The example combines a strict quadratic condition with a non-strict lower bound. Read the intersection of both requirements rather than treating the outputs as alternatives.

The real number line is the domain here. Test boundary points deliberately: $x=1$ satisfies both conditions, while $x=3$ fails the strict quadratic condition. Later, changing a strict sign changes which endpoints belong.

refresher.title: Intervals and strict boundaries
refresher.body: An interval contains a range of real numbers. A strict inequality excludes equality at its boundary.
refresher.example: Combining $x^2<4$ with $x\ge1$ gives $1\le x<2$. The value 2 is excluded, while 1 is included.

lessons.predict: Does $x^2<9$ include either endpoint -3 or 3?
lessons.look: The strict upper boundary is preserved. Mathematical domains and endpoint inclusion are part of the result.
lessons.change: Change <9 to <=9 and compare the boundary check at 3.
lessons.question: What region satisfies $x^2<4$ `together` with $x\ge1$?
options: $-2<x<2$ with no other restriction.
lessons.feedback: Both conditions must hold. The non-strict lower bound includes 1; the strict quadratic bound excludes 2.
hints: Intersect the two permitted regions.
Check each endpoint separately.
lessons.limit: This lesson covers supported univariate real inequalities; coupled multivariate inequality systems require other methods.

lessons.title: A numerical root needs a check
lessons.short: Use nsolve with a starting value and report its local numerical scope.
lessons.goal: Use nsolve with a starting value and report its local numerical scope.
explain: Some equations do not have a convenient elementary solution. `nsolve` approximates a root numerically from a starting value or suitable bracket. A returned root is not automatically a catalogue of all roots.

The residual measures how nearly the original equation is satisfied at the computed value. A small residual is useful evidence, but its relationship to root accuracy depends on sensitivity and conditioning. Verify denominator restrictions and real-world admissibility as well.

The cubic below has three simple roots, so several starting guesses expose the local nature of the calculation. In harder problems, nearby guesses can converge to the same root, fail or encounter singularities. Report the equation, precision, guesses and verification rather than claiming completeness from one run.

refresher.title: Roots and residuals
refresher.body: A root makes $f(x)=0$. A residual is the value f(candidate), which should be close to zero for a numerical candidate.
refresher.example: The exact roots are -1, 0 and 1. One numerical search need not reveal all three.

lessons.predict: Will one starting guess necessarily find every root of $x^3-x$?
lessons.look: The deliberately separated guesses find different roots in this example. That is a demonstration, not a general completeness strategy.
lessons.change: Try cos(x)-x from a starting guess of 1. Check the residual at increased precision.
lessons.question: A single `nsolve` call finds a root. Which claim is justified?
options: It found a numerical candidate from that setup, subject to verification.
It proved there are no other roots anywhere.
The starting value has no effect on numerical solving.
lessons.feedback: Numerical root finding is local and algorithm-dependent. Separate a verified candidate from a complete solution set.
hints: Identify what information the call actually searched.
Check the original residual and domain.
lessons.limit: A small residual alone is not a universal root-error bound, and one successful search does not establish completeness.

lessons.title: Compose functions in the right order
lessons.short: Use Lambda to represent a rule and distinguish two orders of composition.
lessons.goal: Use Lambda to represent a rule and distinguish two orders of composition.
explain: A function maps permitted inputs to outputs. Composing functions means applying one rule to the result of another. The order matters: $f(g(x))$ usually differs from $g(f(x))$.

SymPy `Lambda` represents a symbolic rule with explicit arguments. Calling it with an expression substitutes that expression into its argument position. This makes composition inspectable without creating a numerical Python function yet.

The example compares adding one then squaring with squaring then adding one. Evaluate both at the same input and compare their formulas. Keep a function’s domain in mind: a formal composition may require an output of the inner function to lie inside the outer function’s permitted inputs.

refresher.title: Function notation
refresher.body: f(x) means the output of the rule f at input x. Composition feeds an output into another rule.
refresher.example: At $x=2$, $g(f(2))=9$ while $f(g(2))=5$. Function order changes the result.

lessons.predict: Do “add one, then square” and “square, then add one” define the same rule?
lessons.look: Read nested calls from the inside outward. Both rules are defined for all real inputs in this example.
lessons.change: Replace the rule $f(x)$ with $f(x)=2x$ and repeat. Find an input where the two compositions differ.
lessons.question: In $h(k(x))$, which rule receives x first?
options: h
Both simultaneously.
k
lessons.feedback: The inner call k(x) is evaluated as the input expression for h. That order is part of the definition.
hints: Start at the innermost parentheses.
Track the output passed to the next rule.
lessons.limit: This example uses polynomial rules. Compositions involving roots or logarithms need explicit domain checks.

lessons.title: Use a trigonometric identity
lessons.short: Apply trigsimp and keep angle units explicit.
lessons.goal: Apply trigsimp and keep angle units explicit.
explain: Sine and cosine connect an angle with coordinates on the unit circle. SymPy’s trigonometric functions use radians. An exact angle such as $\pi/6$ preserves identities that may be obscured by an early decimal approximation.

`trigsimp` can recognise combinations of trigonometric functions. In the example, the Pythagorean identity reduces a sum of squares to one. This is a mathematical identity, unlike the empirical observation that a few numerical evaluations happen to match.

Convert degrees explicitly when needed by multiplying by $\pi/180$. The plain number 30 means thirty radians to sin, not thirty degrees. Keep the angle unit attached to input descriptions, especially when connecting a symbolic expression to external data or a numerical array.

refresher.title: Radians and the unit circle
refresher.body: A full turn is 2π radians or 360 degrees. On the unit circle, sine and cosine give coordinates whose squared lengths add to one.
refresher.example: $\sin(\pi/6)=1/2$ exactly. Passing the number `30` without conversion asks for sine of thirty radians.

lessons.predict: Will `sp.sin(30)` mean sine of thirty degrees?
lessons.look: The exact angle gives an exact half. Radian conversion is part of the input model.
lessons.change: Calculate cos(60 degrees) exactly and compare with cos(60 radians).
lessons.question: A table gives angles in degrees. What should happen before using SymPy sin?
options: Convert each angle to radians explicitly.
Assume sin detects the unit from its magnitude.
Round every angle to an integer.
lessons.feedback: Trigonometric functions do not infer units from values. Explicit conversion keeps the calculation meaningful.
hints: One full turn has two common numerical descriptions.
Multiply degrees by π/180.
lessons.limit: Symbolic identities do not compensate for incorrect angle units or an unsuitable geometric model.

lessons.title: Respect logarithm branches
lessons.short: Use positivity assumptions when expanding logarithms and identify a complex counterexample.
lessons.goal: Use positivity assumptions when expanding logarithms and identify a complex counterexample.
explain: A logarithm reverses exponentiation, but its domain and branch matter. For positive real inputs, $\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$. Extending that rule carelessly to complex values can change the answer by multiples of $2\pi i$.

SymPy uses the principal logarithm for complex inputs. The argument chooses a branch, so identities that are valid for positive real numbers cannot automatically be extended to unrestricted complex symbols. State assumptions before expanding a logarithm.

The counterexample uses $a=b=-1$. The product is one, whose principal log is zero, while each principal log of $-1$ is $i\pi$. Avoid `force=True` unless you have separately justified the missing conditions and will preserve them in the result.

refresher.title: Inverse rules have conditions
refresher.body: For positive real numbers, exponentials and logarithms obey familiar inverse rules. Complex logarithms require a branch convention.
refresher.example: For $a=b=-1$, $\log(ab)=\log1=0$ but the sum of the principal logarithms is $2\pi i$. Positivity is doing real work in the identity.

lessons.predict: Is the real-positive product rule automatically valid for every complex pair?
lessons.look: A shorter expression is not useful if it silently changes the branch or domain.
lessons.change: Compare `sp.log(sp.sqrt(z))` for unrestricted $z$ with a positive symbol. State the assumptions beside any rewrite.
lessons.question: What justifies splitting $\log(ab)$ into $\log a+\log b$ in this lesson?
options: The expression contains only two factors.
Both a and b are known positive real numbers.
Calling a general simplifier several times.
lessons.feedback: The assumptions support the identity. Repeated computation cannot supply a missing mathematical condition.
hints: Test the negative pair in the example.
Identify which assumption rules that pair out.
lessons.limit: Complex branch cuts are a larger topic; this example establishes why forced rewrites need explicit justification.

lessons.title: Define a piecewise rule
lessons.short: Build Piecewise with an explicit boundary and fallback branch.
lessons.goal: Build Piecewise with an explicit boundary and fallback branch.
explain: A piecewise function uses different formulas in different regions. Conditions are evaluated in order, and the first applicable branch wins. A final True condition provides an otherwise branch.

The absolute-value example has a negative-input branch and a nonnegative fallback. The point $x=0$ falls in the fallback because the first condition is strict. Writing that boundary deliberately avoids gaps or double interpretations.

Piecewise can represent tariffs, thresholds and physical regimes, but the model must state the permitted inputs and any discontinuities. Inspect representative interior points and exact boundaries before differentiating, integrating or converting the rule into numerical code.

refresher.title: Rules on regions
refresher.body: A piecewise definition states both the formula and the region where it applies. Boundary inclusion is part of the rule.
refresher.example: At -2 use the first branch and obtain 2. At 0 use the second branch and obtain 0.

lessons.predict: Which branch handles $x=0$ when the first condition is $x<0$?
lessons.look: The fallback supplies a value at the boundary. The displayed Abs form expresses the same real function.
lessons.change: Make a delivery tariff costing 5 for order value below 20 and zero otherwise. Test exactly 20.
lessons.question: Two Piecewise conditions both match an input. Which branch is selected?
options: The first applicable branch.
The last applicable branch.
Their average.
lessons.feedback: Order matters. Design overlapping conditions intentionally or rewrite them into clear disjoint regions.
hints: Read Piecewise from top to bottom.
Stop at the first true condition.
lessons.limit: A piecewise rule needs its own domain and boundary checks; a symbolic definition alone does not validate a real tariff or regime change.

lessons.title: Read a polynomial and its roots
lessons.short: Use Poly and roots to distinguish degree, coefficients and multiplicity.
lessons.goal: Use Poly and roots to distinguish degree, coefficients and multiplicity.
explain: A polynomial in x is a finite sum of nonnegative integer powers of x with coefficients. Poly makes the chosen polynomial variable explicit, which matters when other symbols act as parameters.

The degree is the highest power with a nonzero coefficient. A root can occur more than once: multiplicity records how many copies of its factor appear. The roots function returns a mapping from discovered roots to multiplicities for this tractable example.

Inspect the expanded coefficients, factored expression and root multiplicities `together`. A repeated root may touch rather than cross the horizontal axis in a real plot. General polynomial equations need not have simple radical forms, so do not assume a small explicit roots mapping always describes every possible problem.

refresher.title: Repeated factors
refresher.body: A root r corresponds to a factor x-r. Repeating that factor creates a root with higher multiplicity.
refresher.example: The polynomial has degree 3. Root 1 has multiplicity 2 and root -2 has multiplicity 1; the multiplicities total 3.

lessons.predict: Does a repeated root count only once towards the degree?
lessons.look: all_coeffs includes zero coefficients for missing intermediate powers. Multiplicity carries information beyond the distinct root list.
lessons.change: Replace the repeated factor by `(x-1)**3` and predict the new degree and multiplicity.
lessons.question: A degree-four polynomial has a root with multiplicity three. How much degree does that factor account for?
options: One.
Three.
Four, regardless of all other factors.
lessons.feedback: The factor (x-r)³ contributes three to the polynomial degree even though r is one distinct root value.
hints: Expand the repeated factor as a power.
Multiplicity counts repeated linear factors.
lessons.limit: Exact radical roots are not available for all polynomials; RootOf-style descriptions or numerical roots may be appropriate.

lessons.title: Sum a family of terms
lessons.short: Represent a finite symbolic sum and evaluate its closed form.
lessons.goal: Represent a finite symbolic sum and evaluate its closed form.
explain: A finite sum adds terms indexed by an integer. SymPy Sum can retain the summation object before evaluating it with doit. This separates the mathematical definition from the closed form a symbolic algorithm can obtain.
The upper endpoint is included in the sum below. Declaring n as a positive integer matches the intended finite-count model. Product uses an analogous notation for multiplication rather than addition.

Compare the symbolic formula with a small hand-checkable case. When moving to infinite sums, convergence becomes an additional mathematical requirement; a finite-sum identity should not be extended by simply replacing n with infinity without checking that requirement.

refresher.title: Sigma notation
refresher.body: The symbol Σ instructs you to add one term for each integer index in the specified range, including both endpoints here.
refresher.example: For $n=4$, the terms are $1+2+3+4=10$, and the formula gives $4\cdot5/2=10$.

lessons.predict: Does `sp.Sum(k,(k,1,4))` include the term $k=4$?
lessons.look: The sum is $10$ at $n=4$, while the product is $24$. Similar index notation can describe different operations.
lessons.change: Sum $k^2$ from $1$ to $n$ and verify the formula at $n=3$.
lessons.question: Before interpreting an infinite-series result, what extra question matters?
options: Whether the sum has more than one symbol.
Whether convergence holds under the stated parameter conditions.
Whether the finite upper endpoint was even.
lessons.feedback: An infinite process needs convergence analysis. Finite identities alone do not supply it.
hints: Finite and infinite addition are different mathematical claims.
Check the conditions under which the infinite total exists.
lessons.limit: This lesson establishes finite indexed operations; infinite-series convergence requires further analysis.

lessons.title: A limit is not a substitution
lessons.short: Distinguish a limiting value from direct evaluation and compare one-sided limits.
lessons.goal: Distinguish a limiting value from direct evaluation and compare one-sided limits.
explain: A limit describes the value approached as an input moves towards a point through permitted nearby values. The function need not be defined at that point. This differs from directly substituting the point into the expression.
SymPy limit can specify approach from the right or left. A two-sided real limit requires those approaches to agree. Infinite one-sided limits with opposite signs do not combine into one finite value.

For sin(x)/x at zero, direct substitution gives an indeterminate expression while the limiting value is one. The reciprocal 1/x illustrates a different behaviour: its left and right limits diverge in opposite directions. Read the direction and domain beside every limit result.

refresher.title: Approaching versus arriving
refresher.body: A limiting value concerns nearby inputs, not necessarily the formula’s value exactly at the point.
refresher.example: For small positive and negative $x$ in radians, $\sin(x)/x$ approaches $1$. The original fraction remains undefined at zero.

lessons.predict: Must an undefined direct substitution imply that no finite limit exists?
lessons.look: The reciprocal limits disagree. The limit of sin(x)/x and its missing point are separate facts.
lessons.change: Compute left and right limits of $|x|/x$ at zero and explain why there is no common two-sided value.
lessons.question: A function’s left and right limits at a point are different. What follows?
options: Their average is the two-sided limit.
The ordinary two-sided real limit does not exist.
Direct substitution must be zero.
lessons.feedback: A common two-sided limit requires agreement. Averaging incompatible approaches changes the question.
hints: Follow the input from each side.
Ask whether both approaches lead to the same value.
lessons.limit: Limits depend on approach and domain; complex limits can require stronger path-independent reasoning.

lessons.title: Differentiate a composed expression
lessons.short: Calculate a derivative and interpret the chain-rule factor.
lessons.goal: Calculate a derivative and interpret the chain-rule factor.
explain: A derivative describes the local rate of change of a function with respect to a chosen variable. SymPy diff applies symbolic differentiation rules to an expression. State the variable explicitly, particularly when parameters appear in the formula.

For a composed function, the chain rule includes the derivative of the inner expression. Differentiating exp(x squared) therefore produces both an exponential factor and a $2x$ factor. Omitting the inner derivative changes the rate.

The example also evaluates the derivative at a specific input. That number describes the slope there, not the function’s value. Units follow the ratio of output units to input units, and a symbolic derivative does not establish whether the original formula accurately models a measured process.

refresher.title: Slope and the chain rule
refresher.body: A derivative measures local change. For a composition, multiply the outer derivative by the derivative of its input.
refresher.example: At $x=1$, the function value is $e$ but its derivative is $2e$. These are different quantities.

lessons.predict: Will differentiating $e^{x^2}$ give only $e^{x^2}$?
lessons.look: The inner derivative $2x$ is visible. A second derivative describes change in the slope.
lessons.change: Change the inner expression to `3*x+1`. Predict the new chain-rule factor.
lessons.question: For $\sin(5x)$, which factor comes from differentiating the inner expression?
options: x
`sin(x)`
lessons.feedback: The derivative of $5x$ with respect to $x$ is $5$, so the derivative is $5\cos(5x)$.
hints: Separate the outer rule from the inner expression.
Differentiate $5x$ first.
lessons.limit: Differentiation is conditional on the formula and variable assumptions; it does not validate a physical or statistical model.

lessons.title: Differentiate an implicit curve
lessons.short: Obtain an implicit derivative and identify where its denominator vanishes.
lessons.goal: Obtain an implicit derivative and identify where its denominator vanishes.
explain: Some relationships define a curve without giving y as one global function of x. Implicit differentiation treats y as changing with x while preserving the relationship. SymPy idiff can calculate that derivative from an equation written as a zero residual.
On a circle, differentiating $x^2+y^2-r^2=0$ with respect to $x$ gives $2x+2y\,dy/dx=0$. Solving for the slope divides by $y$, so the resulting formula requires $y\ne0$.

Inspect slopes at two points on a radius-five circle, then note the missing boundary points where $y=0$. A vertical tangent can fail to have a finite $dy/dx$ even though the curve itself remains well defined. Keep the derivative’s domain distinct from the curve’s domain.

refresher.title: An implicit relationship
refresher.body: An equation can constrain x and y `together` without selecting one y for each x. A circle generally has an upper and a lower branch.
refresher.example: At $(3,4)$ the slope is $-3/4$. At $(5,0)$ this slope formula divides by zero, reflecting a vertical tangent.

lessons.predict: Does division by $y$ in the formula for $dy/dx$ mean the circle itself disappears at $y=0$?
lessons.look: The curve check at $(5,0)$ is zero even though its $dy/dx$ formula is not finite there.
lessons.change: Use the ellipse $x^2+4y^2=16$ and derive its implicit slope.
lessons.question: What should accompany a slope formula containing division by y?
options: A claim that every curve point is invalid.
A restriction y≠0 for that finite-slope formula and analysis of the omitted points.
An instruction to replace $y=0$ with $y=1$.
lessons.feedback: The derivative representation has a local domain. Singular slope points deserve interpretation, not arbitrary substitution.
hints: Locate the denominator.
Separate a valid curve point from the existence of a finite slope.
lessons.limit: Implicit derivatives require local regularity; singular points and branch changes can need additional analysis.

lessons.title: Take one partial derivative at a time
lessons.short: Build a gradient with an explicit order of input variables.
lessons.goal: Build a gradient with an explicit order of input variables.
explain: A function of several variables can change in several directions. A partial derivative changes one input while holding the others fixed. The gradient collects those partial derivatives in a stated variable order.

SymPy diff treats other independent symbols as constants when differentiating with respect to one symbol. Parameters are not automatically functions of that symbol; declare functional dependence explicitly if the model requires it.

The quadratic example has inputs x and y with a cross term. Compute each partial derivative, form a column vector and evaluate it at a point. A zero gradient is a candidate for an interior stationary point; it does not by itself prove a minimum, maximum or feasible solution.

refresher.title: Partial change
refresher.body: A partial derivative varies one coordinate while the other independent inputs stay fixed.
refresher.example: At $(1,2)$, the gradient is $(4,5)$. Its entries refer to $x$ and $y$ respectively.

lessons.predict: When taking the partial derivative of $xy$ with respect to $x$, does $y$ also differentiate to one?
lessons.look: Holding $y$ fixed gives derivative $y$ for $xy$. The vector order must remain attached to its entries.
lessons.change: Add $3xy$ and predict the change to both gradient components.
lessons.question: A function has gradient zero at a point. What has been established?
options: A stationary-point candidate, requiring classification and any constraint checks.
A global minimum in every possible domain.
That the function is constant everywhere.
lessons.feedback: Vanishing first derivatives alone do not classify a point. Curvature, boundaries and constraints matter.
hints: A flat slope can occur at a maximum or saddle as well as a minimum.
Separate finding candidates from classifying them.
lessons.limit: This example assumes independent coordinates and smooth polynomial derivatives; constraints and nonsmooth points require care.

lessons.title: Integrate and check by differentiating
lessons.short: Distinguish an antiderivative family from a definite accumulated quantity.
lessons.goal: Distinguish an antiderivative family from a definite accumulated quantity.
explain: An antiderivative F of f has derivative f. Indefinite integration finds one representative, while adding an arbitrary constant describes the family on a suitable interval. Definite integration instead accumulates signed contributions between specified bounds.

SymPy integrate can perform either operation depending on the arguments. Integral retains an unevaluated mathematical object until doit is requested, which is useful for keeping the problem definition visible.

The example integrates a polynomial, differentiates the result to check it, and evaluates a bounded integral. The derivative check cannot determine an additive constant. For functions with singularities, inspect the integration interval and convergence rather than assuming a symbolic expression guarantees a finite ordinary integral.

refresher.title: Accumulation and antiderivatives
refresher.body: Integration connects a rate with accumulation. Adding a constant to an antiderivative does not change its derivative.
refresher.example: The definite result is $x^2$ evaluated at $3$ minus $x^2$ evaluated at $0$. The arbitrary constant cancels.

lessons.predict: Does the derivative check distinguish $F$ from $F+7$?
lessons.look: The constant belongs in the indefinite family. The definite integral is a number in this example.
lessons.change: Integrate $3x^2$ between 0 and 2. Check the antiderivative separately.
lessons.question: What does differentiating an antiderivative verify?
options: Its additive constant uniquely.
That its derivative matches the integrand on the relevant domain.
That every improper integral of the integrand converges.
lessons.feedback: A derivative verifies the local antiderivative relationship, while constants and improper bounds require separate information.
hints: The derivative of every constant is zero.
Separate a derivative identity from a bounded or improper accumulation.
lessons.limit: General integrals may remain unevaluated or require convergence conditions and piecewise domains.

lessons.title: Keep the remainder in a series
lessons.short: Interpret a Taylor polynomial as a local approximation with an order term.
lessons.goal: Interpret a Taylor polynomial as a local approximation with an order term.
explain: A Taylor expansion approximates a sufficiently smooth function near a chosen point using powers of the displacement from that point. The expansion point and retained order are part of the statement, not optional annotations.

SymPy series includes an Order term describing asymptotic remainder behaviour. removeO extracts a polynomial when you need to evaluate or plot it, but removing the notation does not eliminate the mathematical approximation error.

The sine example expands around zero through powers below seven. Compare its errors at a nearby and a farther input. A small error at one point is a useful check, not a global error bound. Keep the original function available when using a truncated approximation in a model.

refresher.title: Local approximation and big O
refresher.body: A Taylor polynomial matches a function’s derivatives at a chosen point. O(x⁷) describes remainder scaling near zero, not an exact equality everywhere.
refresher.example: At small $|x|$, the first omitted powers can be small. Farther from zero, the same polynomial may be much less accurate.

lessons.predict: Does removeO make a Taylor polynomial exact for every x?
lessons.look: The error grows between these chosen points. This comparison illustrates locality rather than proving a universal monotonic error law.
lessons.change: Expand exp(x) around $x=1$ instead of zero. Identify powers of x-1 in the result.
lessons.question: Which details belong beside a truncated series used in a calculation?
options: Only the number of printed terms.
Only its value at zero.
Expansion point, retained order and a justified range or error assessment.
lessons.feedback: The approximation is tied to a neighbourhood and truncation. Those details determine whether it suits the calculation.
hints: Ask where the polynomial was constructed.
Track what was omitted and where its error is acceptable.
lessons.limit: An asymptotic order term is not by itself a numerical error bound throughout an arbitrary interval.

lessons.title: A matrix acts on a vector
lessons.short: Calculate a matrix-vector product and interpret its rows.
lessons.goal: Calculate a matrix-vector product and interpret its rows.
explain: A matrix is a rectangular arrangement of entries. Multiplying a matrix by a column vector forms one output per row by summing products. This represents a linear transformation when the entries are fixed.

SymPy `Matrix` uses `*` for matrix multiplication, while NumPy array `*` multiplies elements in matching positions. Dimensions must agree: the matrix’s column count matches the vector’s row count. Keep the coordinate order attached to both input and output vectors.

The example shears a two-dimensional vector and then compares two orders of matrix transformations. In general $AB$ and $BA$ differ. An exact symbolic calculation can reveal that order dependence without rounding or a plot.

refresher.title: Rows times columns
refresher.body: Each output entry is a dot product: multiply corresponding entries and add them.
refresher.example: The first row gives $1\cdot3+2\cdot4=11$. The second gives $0\cdot3+1\cdot4=4$.

lessons.predict: Will swapping two matrix transformations always leave the same result?
lessons.look: The transformation nearest the vector acts first. SymPy Matrix multiplication preserves row-column structure.
lessons.change: Replace v with each coordinate basis vector [1,0] and [0,1]. Relate the outputs to A’s columns.
lessons.question: For a 2×3 matrix multiplied by a column vector, what input size is required?
options: Any size if entries are numbers.
lessons.feedback: Three matrix columns require three input entries. The output has two entries because there are two rows.
hints: Match the inner dimensions.
The output size follows the number of matrix rows.
lessons.limit: A matrix model needs meaningful coordinates and units; multiplication alone does not establish a real transformation’s validity.

lessons.title: Rank explains a family of solutions
lessons.short: Relate matrix rank to redundant and inconsistent linear constraints.
lessons.goal: Relate matrix rank to redundant and inconsistent linear constraints.
explain: The rank of a matrix counts independent row or column directions. Redundant equations do not contribute new independent information. Comparing the coefficient matrix with its augmented matrix helps distinguish redundancy from inconsistency.

In the example, the second coefficient row is twice the first. When its right-hand side also doubles, the system has a family of solutions. Changing that right-hand side breaks compatibility without increasing the coefficient rank.

Inspect both `linsolve` outputs and the ranks. A free parameter is meaningful information about what the equations fail to determine; it should not be silently replaced by zero. Additional evidence or constraints are needed to select one member of a family.

refresher.title: Redundant versus conflicting equations
refresher.body: Two equations can say the same thing or contradict one another. Counting written equations is not the same as counting independent constraints.
refresher.example: The second equation repeats the first. Replacing 6 by 7 makes the pair inconsistent, because doubling the first equation must give 6.

lessons.predict: Will two written equations in two unknowns necessarily determine one unique pair?
lessons.look: The family and `EmptySet` describe different mathematical outcomes. Neither is a uniquely solved pair.
lessons.change: Add an independent equation $x-y=1$ and solve the compatible system again.
lessons.question: A solution family contains a free parameter. What does it mean?
options: The supplied constraints leave a degree of freedom.
The parameter must automatically equal zero.
The solver necessarily encountered a numerical error.
lessons.feedback: A family describes underdetermination in the mathematical problem. Selecting a value requires an additional reason.
hints: Ask how many independent conditions the equations supply.
A symbol in a family records freedom rather than a mistake.
lessons.limit: Exact rank can change discontinuously with parameter values; approximate numerical rank needs tolerances and conditioning analysis.

lessons.title: Check an inverse by multiplication
lessons.short: Use a determinant and an exact product to establish invertibility in a small example.
lessons.goal: Use a determinant and an exact product to establish invertibility in a small example.
explain: A square matrix is invertible when its transformation can be undone uniquely. Its determinant is nonzero exactly when an inverse exists over the usual field of scalars. A zero determinant signals dependent directions.

For a small exact matrix, inv returns the inverse and multiplication checks that the composition is the identity. Perform the check with the original matrix rather than trusting the appearance of reciprocal-looking entries.

Computing an explicit inverse is not the default way to solve a large numerical system. Appropriate factorisation-based solvers usually serve that task better. Here, exact inversion is a compact way to understand reversibility, singularity and the meaning of the identity matrix.

refresher.title: The identity transformation
refresher.body: The identity matrix leaves every compatible vector unchanged. An inverse undoes another matrix’s action.
refresher.example: Multiplying a vector by $A$ and then by $A^{-1}$ restores that vector when the inverse exists. A zero determinant rules this out.

lessons.predict: Can a matrix with dependent rows have a two-sided inverse?
lessons.look: The exact product is the identity matrix. The dependent-row example has determinant zero.
lessons.change: Change the bottom-right entry of `A` to `sp.Rational(1,2)`. Predict singularity before attempting inversion.
lessons.question: What does a nonzero determinant establish for a square exact matrix?
options: Every entry must be positive.
The matrix is invertible.
The matrix equals its transpose.
lessons.feedback: Invertibility concerns independent directions, not positivity or symmetry of individual entries.
hints: Connect determinant zero with collapsed directions.
A reversible square transformation has no lost direction.
lessons.limit: Numerically tiny determinants alone are poor conditioning diagnostics; floating-point problems need scale-aware analysis.

lessons.title: Find directions that keep their line
lessons.short: Interpret an eigenvector and verify its eigenvalue equation.
lessons.goal: Interpret an eigenvector and verify its eigenvalue equation.
explain: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector whose transformed result remains on the same line. Its eigenvalue is the scalar multiplying that vector. The scalar may stretch, shrink, reverse or, in complex settings, have a broader interpretation.

SymPy `eigenvals` reports eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicity. `eigenvects` also reports bases for the corresponding eigenspaces. An eigenvector’s scale is not unique: any nonzero scalar multiple represents the same direction.

The symmetric matrix below has two real eigenvalues. Check the chosen direction directly by calculating $Av-\lambda v$. This zero-vector residual is clearer evidence than a picture alone. The zero vector is excluded from the definition because it would satisfy that equation for every scalar.

refresher.title: Scaling along a direction
refresher.body: Multiplying a vector by a scalar changes its magnitude and possibly its sign without changing the line it lies on.
refresher.example: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, the vector $(1,1)$ becomes $(3,3)$. Its eigenvalue is $3$, and $(2,2)$ is another eigenvector on the same line.

lessons.predict: Must every eigenvector returned by another implementation have exactly the same scale?
lessons.look: Compare eigenspaces or verified directions rather than requiring one particular vector normalisation.
lessons.change: Verify the direction [1,-1] and identify its eigenvalue.
lessons.question: Why is the zero vector excluded from the eigenvector definition?
options: It has too many coordinates.
It is never a valid matrix input.
It satisfies $Av=\lambda v$ for every λ and identifies no direction.
lessons.feedback: A nonzero vector is needed to associate a meaningful direction with an eigenvalue.
hints: Substitute $v=0$ into both sides.
No scalar can be distinguished that way.
lessons.limit: Eigenvalue multiplicity and eigenspace dimension differ in general; not every square matrix has a full eigenvector basis.

lessons.title: Use a different coordinate basis
lessons.short: Verify diagonalisation before using it to compute a matrix power.
lessons.goal: Verify diagonalisation before using it to compute a matrix power.
explain: A diagonalisation writes $A=PDP^{-1}$, where D is diagonal and the columns of P form an eigenvector basis. In those coordinates, repeated applications reduce to powers of diagonal entries.

Not every square matrix is diagonalizable. Repeated eigenvalues do not by themselves decide the question; the number of independent eigenvectors matters. Check the reconstruction before using a diagonalisation to infer anything else.

The example reconstructs a small symmetric matrix and compares its fifth power with the diagonal-basis calculation. A second matrix demonstrates that diagonalisation is a property to establish rather than an operation guaranteed for every input. This exact example focuses on meaning, not a claim of numerical speed.

refresher.title: Changing coordinates
refresher.body: A basis gives a set of independent coordinate directions. A change of basis describes the same transformation using different coordinates.
refresher.example: The middle $P^{-1}P$ factors cancel in repeated multiplication. The formula requires an invertible P and a valid decomposition.

lessons.predict: Can you use a diagonal-power formula without first establishing a valid eigenvector basis?
lessons.look: Both residual matrices are exactly zero. The Jordan-style example does not admit a complete eigenvector basis.
lessons.change: Change the power to 10 and keep the reconstruction check. Then inspect `J.eigenvects()`.
lessons.question: A repeated eigenvalue appears. What is needed before claiming diagonalizability?
options: A full set of independent eigenvectors.
Only a nonzero top-left entry.
Only a square matrix shape.
lessons.feedback: An invertible eigenvector basis supplies P. Algebraic multiplicity alone does not guarantee enough independent directions.
hints: P must be invertible.
Count independent eigenvectors, not just repeated root labels.
lessons.limit: Exact diagonalisation can be unsuitable or unstable for numerical work; specialised numerical methods may be preferable.

lessons.title: Fit a small line exactly
lessons.short: Solve a least-squares problem and verify the residual’s orthogonality condition.
lessons.goal: Solve a least-squares problem and verify the residual’s orthogonality condition.
explain: An overdetermined linear system may have no exact solution. Least squares chooses coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals. For independent columns, the normal equations set A transpose times the residual to zero.

Use an exact, invented three-point example to keep the geometry inspectable. The coefficient order is intercept then slope. The fitted values need not equal every observation, but the residual vector should be orthogonal to each design column.

The normal-equation solve here is an educational exact calculation. For floating-point data, QR or SVD approaches usually provide better numerical behaviour. A fitted line does not itself establish causation, measurement quality or predictive uncertainty; those require a separate data and model analysis.

refresher.title: Residuals and squared error
refresher.body: A residual is observed minus fitted. Least squares minimises the total of their squares rather than requiring each residual to vanish.
refresher.example: If three points do not lie exactly on one line, a two-parameter line generally leaves nonzero residuals.

lessons.predict: Must every residual be zero at a least-squares solution?
lessons.look: The residual can be nonzero while its projection onto each design column is zero.
lessons.change: Change the observations to [1,2,3] and predict the residual and squared error.
lessons.question: What does a zero $A^T\mathrm{residual}$ establish in this full-column-rank example?
options: The observations were measured without error.
The fitted coefficients satisfy the least-squares normal equations.
The fitted relationship is causal.
lessons.feedback: It verifies an optimisation condition for the mathematical fit, not the provenance or interpretation of the data.
hints: Separate an algebraic check from a scientific claim.
The condition refers to the chosen design matrix and objective.
lessons.limit: Invented inputs and exact normal equations are used. Statistical uncertainty and robust numerical fitting are outside this small derivation.

lessons.title: Optimise inside the permitted region
lessons.short: Compare stationary candidates with feasible boundary values.
lessons.goal: Compare stationary candidates with feasible boundary values.
explain: Optimisation asks for the best value within a stated feasible region. Solving a derivative equal to zero finds interior stationary candidates, but those candidates may be infeasible or may fail to be the desired maximum or minimum.

For a smooth function on a closed bounded interval, examine feasible stationary points and the endpoints. The example maximises $x(10-x)$ on the teaching interval zero to four. Its unconstrained stationary point lies outside that interval.

Keep the objective, feasible domain and candidate evaluation `together`. A solver cannot infer an omitted budget or physical bound from the variable name. More complex constrained problems can need specialised optimisation methods, but this small case makes the boundary issue visible.

refresher.title: Interior points and boundaries
refresher.body: An optimum can occur at a flat interior point or at an edge where movement is restricted.
refresher.example: The stationary point is $x=5$. On $0\le x\le4$ it is not feasible; comparing the feasible boundaries gives the maximum at $x=4$.

lessons.predict: Can the derivative-zero point be rejected because the model does not permit that input?
lessons.look: A mathematically valid stationary point does not become a feasible decision automatically.
lessons.change: Change the upper bound to 8 in both the candidate list and feasibility condition. Predict whether $x=5$ becomes relevant.
lessons.question: An unconstrained optimum violates a physical bound. What should you report?
options: The unconstrained point as the final decision anyway.
A feasible optimum found by considering the bound and other admissible candidates.
That optimisation is impossible for every bounded problem.
lessons.feedback: Constraints define the decision problem. Retain their effect when selecting and reporting an optimum.
hints: Check whether each candidate belongs to the permitted region.
Include boundaries when the domain includes them.
lessons.limit: This closed-interval polynomial permits a complete candidate check; general constrained optimisation can be much harder.
lessons.kind: Exact optimisation of an authored model

lessons.title: Derive motion from an acceleration
lessons.short: Integrate a constant acceleration model and verify its initial conditions.
lessons.goal: Integrate a constant acceleration model and verify its initial conditions.
explain: A model relates mathematical quantities under explicit assumptions. Constant acceleration means velocity changes linearly with time and position changes quadratically. Integrating introduces constants that are fixed by initial velocity and position.

Use separate symbols for time, acceleration and initial conditions. The derivation below constructs velocity and position, then checks both the second derivative and values at time zero. Those checks establish the mathematical consistency of the chosen model.

Units remain part of the interpretation: time in seconds, position in metres, velocity in metres per second and acceleration in metres per second squared. Plain symbols do not enforce dimensional consistency automatically. Changing acceleration, drag, collisions or coordinate conventions would change the model.

refresher.title: Position, velocity and acceleration
refresher.body: Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
