refresher.example: At $t=0$ the formulas give $v_0$ and $s_0$. Differentiating position twice returns $a$.

lessons.predict: Does integrating an acceleration determine the initial position without extra information?
lessons.look: The integration constants encode conditions that acceleration alone does not specify.
lessons.change: Substitute $s_0=0$, $v_0=5$ and $a=-2$. Solve for the time when velocity first reaches zero, then check its admissible sign.
lessons.question: Which information fixes both constants for this second-order position model?
options: Only the units used for time.
Only the random seed.
An initial position and an initial velocity.
lessons.feedback: Two integrations introduce two constants. Position and velocity conditions at a specified time determine them here.
hints: Count how many integrations occur.
Each independent constant needs a corresponding condition.
lessons.limit: The model assumes constant acceleration and consistent units. The symbolic checks do not establish that a real trajectory follows it.
lessons.kind: Exact derivation of an authored motion model

lessons.title: Solve a decay equation
lessons.short: Solve a first-order ODE with an initial condition and verify it.
lessons.goal: Solve a first-order ODE with an initial condition and verify it.
explain: An ordinary differential equation relates a function to its derivatives with respect to one independent variable. A decay law says the rate of change is proportional to the current amount, with a negative sign for loss.

SymPy `Function` represents the unknown function, and `dsolve` seeks a symbolic solution. An initial condition such as $N(0)=N_0$ selects a member of the general solution family. Positive k makes this example decay as time increases.

Use `checkodesol` to substitute the returned function and its derivatives into the original differential equation. Also inspect the initial value. These mathematical checks do not establish that a constant decay rate is a suitable description of an actual population, stock or concentration.

refresher.title: Rate proportional to what remains
refresher.body: Exponential decay removes a constant fraction per unit time rather than a constant absolute amount.
refresher.example: For $k>0$, the half-life is $\log(2)/k$. Doubling $N_0$ doubles the trajectory but leaves that half-life unchanged.

lessons.predict: Will a positive decay rate k make the solution grow or shrink for positive time?
lessons.look: The check reports whether substitution satisfies the ODE. The initial condition supplies separate information.
lessons.change: Double k and compare the symbolic half-life and amount at a fixed positive time.
lessons.question: A general ODE solution contains an arbitrary constant. What typically selects a particular trajectory here?
options: An initial value at a stated time.
A prettier printing format.
Changing the name of the function.
lessons.feedback: The initial condition constrains the otherwise free constant. Labels and rendering do not supply that information.
hints: Many exponential curves satisfy the same proportional-rate law.
Identify which one passes through the specified starting point.
lessons.limit: A first-order constant-rate model omits changing rates, external inputs and measurement uncertainty.
source: SymPy · Solve an ordinary differential equation
lessons.kind: Exact solution of an authored decay model

lessons.title: Derive a charging response
lessons.short: Solve a forced linear ODE and interpret its time constant and limiting value.
lessons.goal: Solve a forced linear ODE and interpret its time constant and limiting value.
explain: An RC charging model balances the input voltage with the capacitor voltage and a derivative term. Under an ideal constant-voltage input, $RC$ sets the characteristic time scale. The zero initial voltage supplies the starting condition.

Represent the unknown voltage as a function of time and solve the first-order ODE. Positive resistance and capacitance support the expected stable response. Check the solution against the equation, its initial value and its long-time limit.

This is an idealised model with authored symbolic parameters, not an electrical measurement. Real components have tolerances, nonideal behaviour and operating limits. A symbolic solution is useful because it exposes which parameter combinations govern the response, while leaving validation of the circuit model as a separate task.

refresher.title: Approaching an equilibrium
refresher.body: A stable first-order response can approach a target exponentially. A time constant is the time scale in the exponential’s denominator.
refresher.example: At $t=0$ the voltage is 0. At $t=RC$ it reaches $V(1-e^{-1})$, about 63.2% of the final value.

lessons.predict: Will the ideal long-time capacitor voltage depend on R if V is held fixed?
lessons.look: $RC$ changes how quickly the response approaches V. It does not change the ideal equilibrium in this model.
lessons.change: Set a nonzero initial voltage in ics and inspect how the transient term changes.
lessons.question: What does increasing R with C fixed change in the ideal model?
options: Only the printed units.
The time constant and transient speed.
The constant input voltage V itself.
lessons.feedback: The parameter product $RC$ controls the exponential time scale. The input V remains the stated external forcing.
hints: Inspect the exponential denominator.
Keep the input definition separate from the system parameters.
lessons.limit: This ideal lumped circuit excludes tolerances, parasitics, nonlinear components and any safety or hardware design assessment.
source: SymPy · Solve an ordinary differential equation
lessons.kind: Exact solution of an idealised circuit model

lessons.title: Integrate a probability density
lessons.short: Check a density’s total mass and calculate an expectation on its stated support.
lessons.goal: Check a density’s total mass and calculate an expectation on its stated support.
explain: A continuous probability density assigns probability through integrals over intervals. Its height is not the probability of a single point. A valid density must be nonnegative and have total mass one over its support.

Use the authored density $2x$ between zero and one, and zero elsewhere. Symbolic integration checks its normalisation and calculates its mean and variance. The integration limits encode the support and must not be discarded.

An expectation weights each value by the density before integrating. The variance is the second moment minus the square of the mean. These exact answers can later benchmark numerical integration or Monte Carlo, but they describe this chosen teaching distribution rather than measured population evidence.

refresher.title: Density versus probability
refresher.body: Probabilities are areas under a density. A density can exceed one at a point while its total integral remains one.
refresher.example: The density reaches 2 at $x=1$, but the probability of an interval is its area, not that endpoint height.

lessons.predict: Does a density value of 2 necessarily make the probability model invalid?
lessons.look: The function is being used as a density only on [0,1]. Outside that interval this model assigns density zero.
lessons.change: Replace $2x$ with `c*x**2` and solve for c so the total mass on [0,1] equals one.
lessons.question: How is $P(a<X<b)$ obtained from a continuous density f?
options: Read f(b) alone.
Multiply f(a) by f(b).
Integrate f from a to b within the support.
lessons.feedback: The integral accumulates probability mass. Individual density heights are not point probabilities.
hints: Think of area under the curve.
Use the relevant interval and support.
lessons.limit: Nonnegativity and normalisation are mathematical checks; they do not validate an assumed distribution against real data.
lessons.kind: Exact calculation for an authored density

lessons.title: Propagate small input uncertainty
lessons.short: Use a Jacobian for a first-order covariance approximation and state its limits.
lessons.goal: Use a Jacobian for a first-order covariance approximation and state its limits.
explain: A nonlinear model can transform uncertainty in several inputs into related output uncertainties. Near a nominal point, the Jacobian collects partial derivatives that describe the local linear response. Multiplying $J\Sigma J^T$ propagates an input covariance matrix through that linear approximation.

The example uses rectangle length and width with independent, invented variances. Its outputs are area and perimeter. Even independent inputs can produce correlated outputs because both outputs depend on the same lengths.

Evaluate the Jacobian at the nominal input before applying the covariance formula. The result is first-order propagation, not an exact uncertainty law for every nonlinear transformation. Large spread, skewness, boundaries and dependence can make a simulation or richer analysis necessary.

refresher.title: Variance, covariance and local change
refresher.body: Variance is squared spread. Covariance describes joint variation; it is not the same as standard deviation.
refresher.example: For one output $y\approx ax+b$, the variance is $a^2$ times the input variance. Multiple outputs can share covariance through common inputs.

lessons.predict: Can area and perimeter be correlated even if length and width errors are independent?
lessons.look: The off-diagonal entry records shared output variation. All input variances and nominal dimensions are invented.
lessons.change: Add a justified nonzero off-diagonal input covariance and compare the propagated area variance.
lessons.question: When is this first-order result most in need of further checking?
options: When nonlinear effects are substantial across the input uncertainty range.
Whenever exact fractions are printed.
Only when the two input names are the same length.
lessons.feedback: The Jacobian describes local linear behaviour. It can miss curvature and distribution shape across a broad range.
hints: Ask whether one local slope represents the whole uncertain region.
Compare with a suitable simulation when curvature matters.
lessons.limit: This is a local approximation using invented independent input uncertainty, not a calibrated confidence interval for a measured rectangle.
lessons.kind: First-order propagation of invented input uncertainty

lessons.title: Turn a formula into a numerical function
lessons.short: Use lambdify with an explicit argument order and numerical backend.
lessons.goal: Use lambdify with an explicit argument order and numerical backend.
explain: A symbolic expression is useful for derivation; a numerical function is convenient for repeated evaluation. `lambdify` translates a SymPy expression into a callable using a selected numerical library. It does not compile or prove the model automatically.

State the argument order explicitly. A function created for (x,a) expects x first and a second. Choose a backend such as math for ordinary scalar calls or numpy for array work. Keep the symbolic expression as the derivation and verification record.

Compare the numerical result with exact symbolic substitution at a check point. The numerical function generally uses floating-point arithmetic, so agreement is approximate and precision follows that backend. Only `lambdify` expressions you trust; this translation uses generated executable code.

refresher.title: A rule and its implementation
refresher.body: A formula defines an input-output relationship. A numerical function implements that rule with a particular argument order and arithmetic.
refresher.example: Swapping the inputs gives $f(2,3)=13$. The same two numbers can produce a different answer when their roles change.

lessons.predict: Will the callable infer argument roles from the numeric values passed to it?
lessons.look: The argument tuple is an interface contract. The backend determines which numerical operations the callable uses.
lessons.change: Add a parameter b, update the argument tuple and verify a new check point by exact substitution.
lessons.question: What should accompany a lambdified function in a reproducible calculation?
options: Only the final decimal output.
Its symbolic source, argument order, backend and numerical checks.
An assumption that it uses exact rational arithmetic.
lessons.feedback: Those details connect the callable to the mathematical rule and make numerical behaviour inspectable.
hints: Write down what each positional input means.
Keep the generating expression and backend explicit.
lessons.limit: `lambdify` uses code generation internally. Use trusted expressions and do not treat arbitrary external strings as safe executable mathematics.

lessons.title: Evaluate a curve on an array
lessons.short: Use a NumPy-backed symbolic function to plot a domain-labelled curve.
lessons.goal: Use a NumPy-backed symbolic function to plot a domain-labelled curve.
explain: A NumPy-backed lambdified function can evaluate many inputs in one call. This connects a symbolic derivation with numerical arrays and plots. Preserve the domain and units when selecting the input grid.

The example plots a known response $e^{-x}$ for nonnegative x. The symbolic expression remains available for exact values, while the plotted samples are floating-point evaluations. A grid is a set of sampled locations, not the whole continuous function.

Plots are useful for interpretation and catching surprising behaviour, but a smooth-looking curve is not a proof of continuity, an identity or exhaustive root coverage. Check exact boundaries and singularities from the symbolic model rather than relying on a finite grid to reveal them.

refresher.title: A graph samples a function
refresher.body: A graph places input on one axis and output on the other. A numerical grid evaluates only its selected inputs.
refresher.example: Sampling between 0 and 4 shows part of the decay. It does not display every nonnegative input or prove a long-time limit.

lessons.predict: Does a plot on 200 points examine every input between the endpoints?
lessons.look: The figure is generated from your actual numerical evaluation. The exact start value and sampled endpoint have different provenance.
lessons.change: Plot `sp.sin(x)` over zero to $2\pi$. Label the horizontal axis in radians and compare two grid sizes.
lessons.question: A plotted curve seems to cross zero once. What further work supports a claim about all roots?
options: Assume the finite grid has proved uniqueness.
Change only the line colour.
Analyse the mathematical domain and equation, with appropriate symbolic or numerical verification.
lessons.feedback: Sampling can miss crossings, tangencies or narrow features. A root claim needs evidence suited to the full domain.
hints: Think about what lies between grid points.
Use the formula and domain, not just the drawing.
lessons.limit: Finite plotting grids can conceal singularities and narrow features; this smooth bounded example deliberately avoids those difficulties.

lessons.title: Rewrite a cancellation-prone calculation
lessons.short: Compare equivalent formulas whose floating-point behaviour differs.
lessons.goal: Compare equivalent formulas whose floating-point behaviour differs.
explain: Subtracting nearly equal numbers can lose significant digits in floating-point arithmetic. Two exactly equivalent symbolic formulas can therefore behave very differently when evaluated numerically. Simplification for readability and reformulation for numerical stability are related but distinct tasks.

For $\sqrt{x+1}-\sqrt{x}$ at large positive x, the two square roots are close. Multiplying by the conjugate gives $\frac1{\sqrt{x+1}+\sqrt{x}}$, which avoids subtracting those nearly equal values. The real-positive domain justifies the manipulation here.

Compare both ordinary scalar implementations with a high-precision reference built from an exact integer input. A successful example demonstrates this specific instability; it is not a general guarantee that every algebraic rewrite improves every calculation. Retain the identity and the numerical check `together`.

refresher.title: Rationalising a difference
refresher.body: Multiplying by a conjugate can replace a small difference with a product identity. Denominators must remain valid.
refresher.example: The numerator after multiplying by the conjugate is $(x+1)-x=1$. The new denominator adds positive quantities instead of subtracting nearly equal ones.

lessons.predict: Can two mathematically equal formulas produce different ordinary floating-point answers?
lessons.look: The direct float calculation can lose the small difference entirely. High-precision evaluation uses the exact input and a separate arithmetic strategy.
lessons.change: Compare inputs `10**4`, `10**8` and `10**16`. Identify when the direct result becomes unreliable.
lessons.question: A symbolic identity is established. What remains to check before choosing a numerical implementation?
options: Floating-point conditioning, stability and the input range.
Only whether both expressions print in one line.
Nothing; exact equivalence guarantees identical rounding.
lessons.feedback: Mathematical equivalence does not imply identical finite-precision evaluation paths.
hints: Inspect operations that subtract close values.
Compare with a suitable higher-precision or exact reference.
lessons.limit: The rewrite is justified on this positive domain and addresses one cancellation mechanism; general numerical stability needs broader analysis.

lessons.title: Precision starts with the input
lessons.short: Construct high-precision decimal inputs before irreversible low-precision evaluation.
lessons.goal: Construct high-precision decimal inputs before irreversible low-precision evaluation.
explain: Requesting more digits does not manufacture information that an input has already lost. A Python float such as 0.1 is an approximate binary number. Passing it to a high-precision constructor preserves that already-rounded value with additional representation, rather than recovering an exact decimal tenth.

A decimal string can specify the intended digits directly, while `Rational(1,10)` expresses an exact mathematical tenth. Choose between them based on what the input means. An instrument’s stated uncertainty still limits an interpretation even if its printed reading has many digits.

Compare errors relative to an exact tenth using fifty-digit arithmetic. This separates input construction from later numerical evaluation. When a formula is sensitive to its inputs, input uncertainty and arithmetic error both deserve explicit checks.

refresher.title: Significant information
refresher.body: An input representation carries a finite amount of information. Extra output digits cannot recover digits discarded earlier.
refresher.tex: 0.1=\frac1{10}\quad\text{exactly as a decimal, but not exactly in binary floating point}
refresher.example: `Float("0.1",50)` starts from decimal text at the requested precision. `Float(0.1,50)` starts from the already rounded Python float.

lessons.predict: Will `Float(0.1,50)` and `Float("0.1",50)` necessarily encode the same fifty-digit value?
lessons.look: The text-based `Float` is still finite-precision arithmetic. `Rational` is the exact mathematical reference, not a claim of exact physical measurement.
lessons.change: Try an input with twenty supplied decimal digits using a string and an ordinary Python numeric literal.
lessons.question: What is the best way to preserve a supplied long decimal literal for high-precision arithmetic?
options: Convert it to a Python float first.
Pass its original decimal text with an appropriate precision.
Round it to two places and request 80 digits later.
lessons.feedback: Construct the input before low-precision rounding occurs. The resulting numerical accuracy is still limited by the source information.
hints: Identify the first irreversible rounding step.
Keep the original digits as text until constructing the high-precision number.
lessons.limit: Arbitrary precision addresses arithmetic representation, not unknown measurement errors or an incorrect mathematical model.

lessons.title: Export an expression as code
lessons.short: Inspect generated C code and separate printing from compilation and validation.
lessons.goal: Inspect generated C code and separate printing from compilation and validation.
explain: A symbolic derivation can produce an implementation in another language. SymPy code printers translate supported expressions into source text. The output remains a representation that needs a host function, declarations, libraries and tests in the target environment.

The example generates a C expression for a simple formula and its derivative. The browser is running Python here; it is not compiling or benchmarking C. The printed code may use functions such as pow whose declarations and linking requirements belong to the target toolchain.

Retain the symbolic expression, its assumptions and reference values alongside generated code. Before deploying it, compile in the intended environment and compare numerical behaviour over the supported range. Code generation transfers a formula; it does not establish units, input validity or numerical stability automatically.

refresher.title: One formula, several representations
refresher.body: Mathematical notation, a SymPy expression and C source can describe the same rule using different syntax and arithmetic conventions.
refresher.example: A C printer may emit `pow(x, 2)+1.0/3.0`. That source text still needs compilation before it becomes an executed C calculation.

lessons.predict: Does seeing generated C text mean that C has been compiled or run in this lesson?
lessons.look: Only the symbolic Python calculation is executed. The C text is a generated artefact for later validation.
lessons.change: Generate code for $e^{-x}$ and identify any standard-library function the target implementation needs.
lessons.question: Which step is still needed after printing target-language source?
options: Compilation and numerical validation in the intended target environment.
Assuming it is already faster than Python.
Discarding the symbolic source and domain.
lessons.feedback: Printing is one stage in an implementation workflow. Execution, performance and correctness claims require actual target-side evidence.
hints: Distinguish a string of source from a running program.
Validate with the compiler and libraries you intend to use.
lessons.limit: This lesson does not compile C or make performance claims; complex code-generation systems require more tooling and tests.

lessons.title: Publish a checked symbolic investigation
lessons.short: Export an investigation linking a question, assumptions, derivation and independent checks.
lessons.goal: Export an investigation linking a question, assumptions, derivation and independent checks.
explain: A reproducible symbolic investigation preserves the question, permitted inputs, exact source, chosen transformations and verification. A short final expression is useful only when its assumptions and interpretation remain visible.

Choose one of the starter tasks in the code: a bounded optimisation, an initial-value ODE or a probability integral. Each starts from an authored teaching model and includes a check. You can replace the starter entirely when your own question needs a different model.

Use the report fields to explain your reasoning before exporting the exact run and a Markdown record. Distinguish symbolic checks from numerical spot checks, and both from evidence that a model describes reality. A result that exposes a missing assumption or leaves a question unresolved is a valid outcome to document.

refresher.title: A checked result has a boundary
refresher.body: A mathematical conclusion applies under stated assumptions. A verification should address the original question rather than only the final printed form.
refresher.example: For an optimum, record the domain and boundary analysis. For an ODE, check the equation and initial condition. For a density, check support and total mass.

lessons.predict: Could a correct symbolic manipulation still answer the wrong modelling question?
lessons.look: The source records the starter model and its restrictions. Your report supplies the question and justification for using it.
lessons.change: Complete a report for one starter, then change the assumptions and describe which checks must change.
lessons.question: What makes a final symbolic result meaningfully reproducible?
options: A screenshot of the shortest formula alone.
The final decimal with no input record.
The source, assumptions, domain, versions, checks and interpretation preserved `together`.
lessons.feedback: Those records let another person examine both the calculation and the claim it supports.
hints: Ask what another person would need to rerun and challenge the result.
Preserve the original model and the verification, not just the answer.
lessons.limit: Starter models are authored examples. Mathematical checks do not establish empirical validity, and an independent project takes longer than this guided initial pass.
lessons.kind: Reproducible investigation with authored starter models

applications.title: Design an open box
applications.short: Combine algebra, constrained optimisation and numerical plotting in a checked design.
applications.goal: Combine algebra, constrained optimisation and numerical plotting in a checked design.
explain: Cutting equal squares from the corners of a rectangular sheet and folding the sides produces an ideal open box. Its volume depends on the cut size. The sheet dimensions below are invented teaching inputs in centimetres, and material thickness is ignored.

Derive the volume, state the permitted cut interval, find stationary candidates and compare the feasible interior with limiting boundaries. An unconstrained algebraic root outside the interval is not a possible cut. Keep the exact optimum before approximating it for a practical reading.

Plot the volume over the full feasible interval as an interpretation aid, while retaining the derivative and boundary checks as mathematical evidence. Extend the report with tolerances, thickness, manufacturing constraints or cost only when the model states how those affect the objective.

refresher.title: A volume from changing dimensions
refresher.body: Box volume is height times length times width. Folding a cut of size x removes x from both ends of each original sheet dimension.
refresher.example: The width becomes zero at $x=4$, so that endpoint is not a useful box. A stationary point beyond 4 cannot be a feasible design.

applications.predict: Can the larger algebraic stationary root be used as a cut even if it exceeds the sheet’s half-width?
applications.look: The plot includes degenerate endpoints for context. The actual box domain is open, and the reported optimum lies strictly inside it.
applications.change: Change the sheet to 15 by 9 cm and update the domain and boundary checks along with the formula.
applications.question: A manufacturing rule requires cuts in half-centimetre increments. What must change?
options: Choose the continuous optimum without considering the rule.
Evaluate admissible discrete cuts, using the continuous result only as useful context.
Assume rounding to the nearest cut always proves the best feasible volume.
applications.feedback: The feasible action set has changed. Compare the permitted discrete choices rather than silently applying an unconstrained continuous answer.
hints: List the cuts the manufacturing rule permits.
Evaluate their actual objective values.
applications.limit: The sheet is invented and ideal: thickness, fold radius, tolerances, waste and structural strength are omitted.

applications.title: Check a projectile model
applications.short: Derive, verify and plot an ideal vertical trajectory with a physical time domain.
applications.goal: Derive, verify and plot an ideal vertical trajectory with a physical time domain.
explain: An ideal vertical launch with constant downward acceleration gives a quadratic height curve. The model below starts at ground height with upward speed v0. The acceleration parameter g is positive, and the minus sign establishes the chosen upward-positive coordinate convention.

Find the nonzero return-to-ground time and the apex time, then verify acceleration and initial conditions. The zero root is the launch event, not a second completed flight. Restrict the plotted physical flight to the interval from launch to return.

The numerical values are invented teaching choices. Treat 9.81 as a modelling convention for g here, not an infinitely precise environmental measurement. Air resistance, changing gravity, obstacles and uncertainty need explicit additions before this becomes an appropriate prediction for a real experiment.

refresher.title: A trajectory has a time domain
refresher.body: A quadratic formula can be evaluated beyond the physical event it models. A return to ground can define the end of the intended flight.
refresher.example: The roots of height are $t=0$ and $t=2v_0/g$. The derivative vanishes halfway between them, at the apex.

applications.predict: Should the root $t=0$ be reported as the completed flight’s return time?
applications.look: The symbolic checks and the plotted interval address different parts of the model: the differential rule, initial state and physical observation boundary.
applications.change: Add an initial height $h_0>0$. Re-solve the ground equation and justify which root represents a future landing.
applications.question: A valid algebraic time root is negative. What does that imply for a model restricted to t≥0?
options: It can be excluded from the physical future-time question, with that restriction stated.
It must be changed to its absolute value.
Every other root is automatically wrong.
applications.feedback: A domain restriction can exclude a mathematical root. Taking an absolute value instead changes the equation’s solution.
hints: Keep algebraic validity separate from physical admissibility.
Check the stated time origin and allowed interval.
applications.limit: This ideal one-dimensional trajectory omits drag and parameter uncertainty and has not been validated against measurements.
applications.kind: Integrated model with invented launch inputs

applications.title: Plan a circuit threshold time
applications.short: Derive a threshold-crossing formula from an ideal response and check it by substitution.
applications.goal: Derive a threshold-crossing formula from an ideal response and check it by substitution.
explain: An ideal RC circuit provides a simple model where symbolic derivation, solving and numerical plotting reinforce one another. Starting with zero capacitor voltage, its charging response approaches a constant input V on time scale $RC$.

Solve for the time to reach half the final voltage, using positive parameters and a nonnegative physical time. Substitute the derived time into the original response to verify the threshold. The symbolic result shows which parameter combinations influence the timing and which cancel.

The selected resistance, capacitance and voltage are invented demonstration inputs. Component tolerances would create uncertainty in the crossing time even when the algebra is exact. Use the report to distinguish the ideal result, the numerical illustration and any evidence needed for a practical timing specification.

refresher.title: A threshold solves an equation
refresher.body: A crossing time is an input t for which the response reaches a specified level. It must lie in the permitted time domain.
refresher.example: Because $V>0$, it cancels from this half-voltage equation. Doubling R with C fixed doubles the ideal crossing time.

applications.predict: Will doubling V alone change the time to reach one half of that same V in the ideal model?
applications.look: The timing formula is independent of V for this relative threshold. That does not mean every absolute voltage threshold has the same property.
applications.change: Replace $V/2$ with a fixed threshold of 2 volts. State conditions on V for a positive finite crossing.
applications.question: For an absolute threshold above the final voltage V, what does the ideal monotone response imply?
options: A guaranteed finite positive crossing.
No finite crossing within the stated ideal charging model.
A requirement to ignore the threshold value.
applications.feedback: The response approaches V from below. A threshold above that limit is outside its reachable range under these assumptions.
hints: Inspect the response’s initial value and long-time limit.
Compare the threshold with that reachable interval.
applications.limit: The ideal response and invented components omit tolerances, parasitics, load effects and hardware validation.
source: SymPy · Solve an ordinary differential equation
applications.kind: Integrated ideal circuit with invented components

applications.title: Benchmark a Monte Carlo estimate
applications.short: Use an exact symbolic expectation to check a seeded simulation under the same model.
applications.goal: Use an exact symbolic expectation to check a seeded simulation under the same model.
explain: Symbolic calculation can provide a reference for a numerical simulation. The comparison is meaningful only if both methods use the same inputs, domain and target quantity. Here radius is uniformly distributed between one and two, and area is $\pi r^2$.

Integrate over the stated uniform density to obtain exact mean area and variance. Then generate independent radius draws, transform each into area, and estimate the mean and its Monte Carlo standard error. The standard error describes numerical variability of the estimated mean, not the spread of individual areas.

A discrepancy larger than expected prompts inspection of the model translation or calculation. Agreement checks an implementation under this authored probability model; it does not establish that real radii are uniform. Preserve the seed, draw count, exact target, actual result and assumptions in the report.

refresher.title: Spread of outcomes versus error of a mean
refresher.body: Outcome variance describes different possible areas. For independent finite-variance draws, the mean’s standard error is sample SD divided by square root of draw count.
refresher.example: More draws refine the simulated mean. They do not narrow the model’s distribution of possible individual areas.

applications.predict: Will increasing simulation draws reduce uncertainty about whether real radii follow the assumed uniform model?
applications.look: The histogram describes possible areas, while MCSE concerns the average of the simulated areas. Exact and numerical results share the same authored model.
applications.change: Increase draw count by a factor of four and repeat with several seeds. Compare MCSE rather than expecting every estimate to move monotonically closer.
applications.question: A simulated mean agrees closely with the exact model mean. What does that support?
options: That the assumed input distribution must describe real measurements.
That the sampling and calculation agree with this model reference to the assessed precision.
That one million individual areas are nearly identical.
applications.feedback: A reference comparison checks implementation under assumptions. Empirical model validation requires separate evidence.
hints: Separate “does the code implement this model?” from “does this model describe reality?”
Identify what the exact integral assumes.
applications.limit: Independent uniform radii and finite moments are assumed. Agreement cannot validate those assumptions against reality.
applications.kind: Exact model reference and seeded teaching simulation
